[456-458] JOHN WINTHROP TO WILLIAM BRADFORD

WORTHY SIR, I receiued your louing letter, and am much prouocked to express my affections towards you, but straitnes of time forbids me, for my desire is to acquainte you, with the lords greate mercies towards vs, in our preuailing against his, and our enimies; that you may rejoyce, and praise his name with vs. About 80 of our men haueing costed along towards the dutch plantation, (some times by water, but most by land) mett hear, and ther, with some pequents, whom they slew or tooke prisoners. 2 sachems they tooke, and beheaded And not hearing of Sassacous (the cheefe sachem) they gaue a prisoner his life, to goe and find him out. He wente and brought them word wher he was, but Sassacouse suspecting him to be a spie, after he was gone fled away, with some 20 more, to the Mohawkes; so our men missed of him. yet deviding them seules, and ranging vp and downe, as the providence of God guided them (for the Indeans were all gone, saue 3 or 4 And they knew not whither to guid them, or els would not) vpon the 13 of this month, they light vpon a great company of them viz. 80 strong men, and 200 women, and children in a small Indean towne, fast by a hideous swamp, which they all slipped Into before our men could gett to them. Our captains were not then come together, but ther was mr. Ludlow, and Captaine Masson, with some 10 of their men, and Captaine Patrick with some 20 or more of his; who shooting at the Indeans, Captaine Trask with 50 more came soone in at the noyse; then they gaue order to surround the swampe, it being aboute a mile aboute; but Leutenante Dauenporte, and some 12 more, not hearing that cammand, fell into the swampe among the Indeans. the swampe was so thicke with shrub woode, and so boggie with all, that some of them stuck fast, and receiued many shott. Leutenant Dauenport was dangerously wounded about his armehole and another shott in the head, so as fainting, they were in great danger to haue been taken by the Indeans; but Sargante Rigges, and Jeffery and 2 or 3 more rescued them, and slew diuerse of the Indeans, with their swords. After they were drawne out, the Indeans desired parley; and were offered (by Thomas Stanton, our Interpretour) that if they would come out, and yeeld them selues, they should haue their liues all that had not their hands in the English blood; whervpon the sachem of the place came forth, and an old man or 2 and theri wiues and chilldren; and after that some other women and children, and so they spake 2 howers, till it was night. then Thomas Stanton was sente into them againe, to call them forth; but they said, they would selle theri liues their, and so shott at him so thicke, as If he had not cried out, and been presently rescued, they had slaine him. Then our men cutt of a place of the swampe with their swords, and cooped the Indeans into so narrow a compass, as they could easier kill them throw the thikets; so they continued all the night, standing aboute 12 foote from an other, and the Indeans coming close vp to our men, shot their arrows so thicke, as they peirced their hatte brimes, and their sleeues and stockins, and other parts of their cloaths, yet so miraculously did the lord preserue them, as not one of them was wounded, saue those 3 who rashly went into the swampe. When it was nere day, it grue very darke, so as those of whem which were left, dropt away betweene our men, though they stood but 12 or 14 foote assunder; but were presenly discouered, and some killed in the pursute. Vpon searching of the swampe the next morning, they found 9 slaine, and some they pulled vp, whome the Indeans had buried in the mire; so as they doe thinke that, of all this company, not 20 did escape, for after they found some, who dyed in their flight, of their wounds receiued. The prisoners were devided, some to those of the riuer, and the rest to vs; of these we send the male children to Bermuda, by mr. William Peirce, and the women and maid children are disposed aboute in the townes. Ther haue been now slaine and taken in all aboute 700. The rest are dispersed, and the Indeans in all quarters so terrified, as all their freinds are affraid to receiue them. 2 of the Sachems of long Iland came to mr. Stoughton and tendered them selues to be tributaries, vnder our protection. And 2 of the Neepnett Sachems haue been with me to seeke our friendship. Amonge the prisoners we haue the wife and children of Mononotto, a womon of a very modest countenance and behaviour. It was by her mediation they they 2 English maids were spared from death, and were kindly vsed by her; so that I haue taken charge of her. One of her first requests was that the English would not abuse her body and that her children might not be taken from her. Those which were wounded were fetched of soone by John Galopp who came with his shalop in a hippie houre, to bring them victuals, and to carrie their wounded men to the pinnass, wher our cheefe surgeon was, mr. Willson, being aboute 8 leagues of. Our people are all in health (the lord be praised) and allthough they had marched in their armes all the day, and had been in fight all the night, yet they professed they found them selues so fresh as they could willingly haue gone to such another bussines.

This is the substance of that which I receiued, though I am forced to omite many considerable circomstances. So being in much straitnes of time (the ship being to departe within this 4 days, and in them the Lord Lee and mr. Vane) I hear breake of, and with harty saluts to, etc. I rest Yours assured

JO: WINTHROP

the 28 of the 5 month 1637

The captains reporte, we haue slaine 13 sachems; but Sassacouse and Monotto are yet liuing.

[2] RUN away from the subscriber, last month, a Negro man of the name of TOM, about 5 feet 6 inches high, of a yellowish complexion, much the appearance of an Indian , has one of his teeth out before, and one of his feet has been much burnt, as also one of his arms, and, as well as I can recollect, on the same side of the foot. His hair is of a different kind from that of a Negro's, rather more of the Indian' s, but partaking of both, which, though short, he frequently ties behind; had on a Russia sheeting coat and breeches, a red cloth jacket, rather the worse for wear, and a white linen shirt. The said slave is by trade a cooper and shoemaker, is remarkably fond of drink, and if indulged, will certainly get drunk, and when so, is apt to be very talkative, is a very artful fellow, and will, I imagine, attempt to pass for a freeman. His connections are mostly in Halifax and Charlotte counties, and, I presume, he will make that way. Whoever will convey the said runaway to me, in Amelia county, living near Rocky Run church, or so secure him that I may get him again, shall have a reward of FIVE POUNDS, besides what the law allows, if taken in Virginia, and if brought from another colony, TEN POUNDS.

DOROTHY JONES.

[796] You have made Inquiry concerned a Slave who you say is taken by our people. We acknowledge to have been of the Company that took him, he is given to Indians who live on a Branch of Susquehannah River, which is called Soghniejadie, therefore we desire you to make a further Inquiry for that place is nearer to you than us.

We desire that this may be forgiven us, there many times happen accidents between one nation and another, but they must not be too hasty, therefore we desire the Govr of Virginia that he may not be too rash to revenge such an Action, which was not committed with design nor by consent of the Sachims, if such things happen between brethren then it must always be lay’d by & reconciled.

You told us not to suffer any of the French Indians to make a path thro' our Country to go fighting, we promise to do our endeavour to prevent them [as much as possible] to approach any of the English Colonies.

We desire also that you may prevent them, for many go fighting thro' Albany to the English Settlements, who do not come thro' the Six Nations.

We desire again that the Governour of Virginia may not be rash, and may lay down the hatchet, which he has in his hands, that he ought to think on the former Treaties which are made between him and the Six Nations, that there ought [not] to be a Quarrel for an action which happen'd not designedly.

record_transcription: [243-244] Wheras Phillip, the late sachem of Paukanakett, and other sachems, his accomplises, having bin in confeaderation and plighted couenant with his maties collonie of New Plymouth, haue lately broken covenant with the English, and they and theire people haue likewise broken out in open rebellion against our sour lord Kinge Charles, his crowne and dignitie, expressed by raising a crewell and vnlawfull warr, murdering his leich people, destroying and burning theire houses and estates, expressing great hostillitie, outrage, and crewellty against his and said maties subjects, wherby many of them were psonally slaine, and some bereaued of theire deare children and relations, among which said rebells an Indian named Popanooie is found to be one, whoe hath had a hand, and is found to be very actiue in the great crewelty and outrage acted vpon seuerall of the inhabitants of the towne of Dartmouth, in the said his maties collonie of New Plymouth, in pticular it being manifest that hee was very actiue towards and about the destruction of seuerall of the children of Thomas Pope, late of Dartmouth aforsaid, and seuerall others of the said towne; in consideration wherof, after due examination had of the pmises, this Court doth heerby condemne and centance him, the said Popanooie, and his wife and children, to ppetuall servitude, they likewise being found coeptenor with him in the said rebellion, and pticularly that hee, the said Popanooie, is to be sold and sent out of the country.

I now send, Thought it my duty to give you an account of what I have – noated down from an Indian Prisoner now onboard this Ship, wch was taken at Pemaquid it being an Examination taken before Capt Davis who is now here present, This Capt of ths Ship seems to be much concerned for the good of the English here, and for that and cam in [illegible], he is not yet determined in his minde whether to leave the prisoner here or to bring him to Boston.

Our soldiers here begin to Inquire for Cloathing Shoes & Blankets, and if you think good to allow them sumthing suitable to make straw beds, our Captaine desires tt some swan shot may be seut, here is wanting about 6 m of shingle nayles to cover the stoar room in the food also a few single & double board - nayles, also a paire of Smiths Bellows, Also I would request your [illegible] Honors to Informate to me what allowance of Rum the soldiers must have, as yet I have allowed them a pint among six men for each day they are upon a March, they Expect the sam while they lie Still being tould by same here present that the Canfrog allows it, please to give me orders what to do in that case, our pork is most part of it Spout, please to give me order to Irrepent coffeee or rather send sutiable effect to purchase the same wch I suppose will be cheaper so to do I suppose Capt Phillips can Inform what goods are sutiable for this place, please to Excuse my rude brevity being in haste remayn.

Your Honors humbly servt

Joseph Prout

record_transcription: [1] Gabriella and her two daughters, Delila and Henrietta, ask the court to enjoin the heirs of Joseph Bell from selling them as slaves . Citing their "history of lineage," they proclaim that Gabriella's grandmother, Jinny, was "an Indian and free" and that her mother, Judy, was "begotten by a white man by whom her grand mother had ten children born at or near Port Royal Caroline Co. Virginia." Jinny resided with one John Roy and, "either by Indenture or some other arrangement," came into the possession of and resided with "a certain Rodham Kenney." After Gabriella was born, she and her mother "were taken by some legal process and sold as the slaves or property of" Kenney and eventually purchased by "a certain Edward Downing," who gave them to his sister, Bell's wife. The Bells then brought them to Tennessee and received the profits of their labor until Joseph died around 1838. The petitioners represent that "there is to be this day an assembling" of Bell's heirs "for the purposes of distributing or selling" them; "the time has at length arrived when complainants are absolutely forced to assert the right which they have to freedom." They reveal that Bell always admitted their ancestors' freedom and that his daughter, Margery, "has repeatedly [2] declared that at her death complainants with their offspring," who now number eight, "should be free." They pray that the court "will decree their absolute freedom and will perpetually enjoin the said defendants from any interference."

Ten Guineas Reward.

ABOUT the 12th of Oct. last, two negro fellows, viz. SHAM AND ABRAHAM, ran away from the subscriber’s plantation on Fenwicke’s Island.

Sham, is about 24 or 25 years of age, of middling stature, but thick and well made; of a yellowish complexion, long bushy hair, speaks good English, and is very artful.

Abraham, is about 20 years of age, 5 feet 8 or 9 inches high, rather slender, of a yellowish complexion; his hair is some what longer and softer than African negroes, but not so long and bushy as Mustees in general. He has a scar, I think, above his right eyebrow, which he got from the kick of a horse, also speaks good English, and is of a mild disposition; they are brothers, and both Mustees.

The above negroes were part of the estate of David Toomer, of Indian land, which belonged to the late Mrs. Gillet; they lived formerly at Indian land, where they have a number of relations and acquaintances, but latterly at Dr. Elijah Gillet’s mills, on Duck Savannah, where it is strongly suspected they are gone, and are harbored by some person in the neighborhood. The above reward shall be given to any person who will deliver said negroes to the subscriber on Edisto Island, or the master of the work house in Charleston, besides twenty guineas, on conviction of any white person or persons harboring them.

WILLIAM CALDER.

January 26.

[84] My two ancestors, John, a Blackhawk Indian brave, and Rachel, a Choctaw maiden, had made themselves a home such as only Indians know, understand, and enjoy. [...]

[85] After a long and dreary journey [from Wabash Valley], the Indians reached Alabama. Rachel had her youngest papoose strapped on her back, while John had cared for the

[86] larger child, Lucy. [...] An older daughter, Courtney, also accompanied her parents. [...] Soon they were in sight of the slave quarters of Patent George’s plantation. The Negroes made the Indians welcome, and the slave dealer allowed them to occupy the cane house; thus the Indians became slaves of Patent George. [...] unhappiness came to the Indian mother [Rachel], for her daughter, Courtney, became the mother of Master Ford George’s child. The parents called the little half-breed "Eliza" and were very fond of her. The widow of John Hawk became the mother of Patent George’s son, Patent Junior. [...] With the wagon trains of Patent and Ford George came Rachel Hawk and her daughters, Courtney, Lucy, and Rachel. Rachel died on the journey from Alabama, but the remaining full-blooded Indians entered Kentucky as slaves. [...]

[87] Suddenly sorrow settled down over the home, and the laughter turned into wailing, for Ford George’s body was found pierced through the heart, and the half-breed, Eliza, was nowhere to be found. [...]

[88] A party of searchers were sent out to look for Eliza. They found her secreted in a canebrake in the low lands of Alabama, nursing her baby boy at her breast. They took Eliza and the baby back to Kentucky. I am that baby, that child of unsatisfactory birth.

[89] Mistress Lorraine [enslaver Ford George’s widow] told the stranger that I had been named in derision, and he suggested she list me in the census as George Fordsman, which she did. [...] My mother’s half-brother, Patent George, allowed his name to be reversed to George Patent when he enlisted in the Union service [...]

[92] When the Civil War broke out [...] My mother took her family and moved away from the plantation, and worked in the broom cane. Soon she discovered that she could not make enough to rear her children, and we were turned over to the court to be bound out.

I was bound out to David Varnell in Livingston County by order of Judge Busch and I stayed there until I was fifteen years of age.

[5] INDENTURING INDIANS - A NICE SYSTEM OF SLAVERY.

RED BLUFF, January 30, 1861.

EDITORS UNION: As the meaning and intent, as well as the consitutionality of the Act passed last Winter in regard to indenturing Indians without their consent, or even apprising them of the fact, but by simply calling on the County or District Judge, with a list, and having him sign it officially-has been doubted by many, I send you a copy of an indenture, now on file in the Clerk's office in Tehama county. The Indians named therein are not prisoners of war, or vagrant Indians, but belong to the Nome Lackee tribe, that have been taught to work, at a cost to Government of about three hundred thousand dollars. And the persons to whom they are indentured have been receiving as salaries from Government, four hundred and seventy-five dollars per month, for nearly four years past.

It may be true that they were in their possesion at that date, as they claimed to be in possession of the Reserve. They were most of them on the Reservation, and not ten per cent. of them have ever seen their humane (?) guardian that "at the instance and request" of Titus and Geiger, made them slaves, without the semblance of a bond to clothe, feed and protect them.

I hope our representatives from this country will attend to this law, and have it either explained or repealed.

from Onboard ths Ship Orang Fine at Falmouth

Haveing but a Minute or two of time now to write, the vesell being at Sayle by whom. I now send, Thought it my duty to give you an account of what I have – noated down from an Indian Prisoner now onboard this Ship, wch was taken at Pemaquid it being an Examination taken before Capt Davis who is now here present, This Capt of ths Ship seems to be much concerned for the good of the English here, and for that and cam in [illegible], he is not yet determined in his minde whether to leave the prisoner here or to bring him to Boston.

Our soldiers here begin to Inquire for Cloathing Shoes & Blankets, and if you think good to allow them sumthing suitable to make straw beds, our Captaine desires tt some swan shot may be seut, here is wanting about 6 m of shingle nayles to cover the stoar room in the food also a few single & double board - nayles, also a paire of Smiths Bellows, Also I would request your [illegible] Honors to Informate to me what allowance of Rum the soldiers must have, as yet I have allowed them a pint among six men for each day they are upon a March, they Expect the sam while they lie Still being tould by same here present that the Canfrog allows it, please to give me orders what to do in that case, our pork is most part of it Spout, please to give me order to Irrepent coffeee or rather send sutiable effect to purchase the same wch I suppose will be cheaper so to do I suppose Capt Phillips can Inform what goods are sutiable for this place, please to Excuse my rude brevity being in haste remayn.

Your Honors humbly servt

Mecurius de Quabacouk

Or

A Declaration of the Dealings of Uncas and the Mohegin Indians to certain Indians, the Inhabitants of Quaba-couk

21. 3. 61

About ten weeks since, Uncas’ son, accompanied with 70 Indians set upon the Indians at Quabacouk, and slew three persons, and carryed away 6 prisoners, among which prisoners was one squa, with her two children, whom when hee had brought to the fort Uncas dismissed the squa, on conditions that shee would goe home, and bring him 25 [pounds] in peage, two guns, and two blankets for the release of herself and her children, which as yet she hath not done, being retained by the Sagamore of the Washakeim, on hopes that their league with the English will free them. At the said time hee carryed away also, in stuffs and monyes, to the value of 37 [pounds] and at such time as Uncas received notice of the displeasure of the English in the Massachusetts, by the Wor[shipful] Mr. Winthrop. He insolently laughed them to scorn and professed that hee would still goe on as hee had begun, and assay who dares to control him. Moreover, 4 days since, there came home a prisoner that escaped, two yet remaining whom Uncas threatens the one of them to kill, and the other to sell away as a slave, and still threatens to continue his war ag[ainst] them notwithstanding any prohibition whatsoever, whose very threats are soe terrible that our Indians dare not wander far from the townes about the Indians, for fear of surprise.

From the relation of Pambasua and testimony of Wasamagin: Quaquequunset and others.

Three things are desired.

First, that Uncas may deliver our prisoners.

Secondly, that hee may return our estates again.

Thirdly, that restitution may be required, for the lives of them slayn.

Researcher note: other transcriptions such as the one on https://nativenortheastportal.com/, mentioned Quabacouk as “Quabaug.” Quaquequunset was the Nipmuc sachem of Quabaug and Pakachoag.

(255) Borderlands families have never had it easy, and the second half of the nineteenth century was no exception. In an act of love and power, American and Hispano families reached out to Indian women and children to ease their borderlands burdens. Lieutenant Colonel King S. Woolsey left his central Arizona ranch in 1864 to kill Apaches and claim land; he returned from his campaign with a ten-year-old Yaqui girl as his personal consort. Lucia Martinez bore the Colonel's children and harassment until his death in 1879. The territorial patriarch left his illegitimate children no inheritance, but he had indentured them, ironically making them eligible for $1,000 from his estate. Woolsey's compatriot Jack Swilling had brandished a gun to uphold slavery, claim Western lands, and make "good Indians," but when his Mexican, American, and O'odham friends staged the Camp Grant Massacre in the spring of 1871, he stayed home with his Mexican wife, four American children, and four Apache wards. Swilling indentured one of these Indian minors, but he most likely did so to protect him from his neighbors' anti-Apache sentiments. Josefina and Miguel Gonzales Roca indentured three-year-old Teutilla in 1869. Of elite families in Mexico and Chile, the Rocas had been nursed and cared for by criadas-mestizo servants-and they wanted the same for their children. When they indentured the Apache toddler, they both continued a longtime Hispanic tradition of dependence upon racially inferior domestics and secured a future of white privilege for their new family.

This chapter focuses on intercultural households to examine linkages between bonds of indenture and ties of affection, between exploitative labor and love, and between questionable paternity and patronage. [131] Report of Brigadier General Scott.

LEXINGTON, 28th June, 1791.

SIR:

I have the honor to inform you that the detachment of mounted volunteers under my command, authorized to be raised by your letter of the 9th of March last, arrived at the mouth of Kentucky on the morning of the 19th of May, from which time to the 23d, I was employed in transporting the troops across the Ohio river, in having them mustered, and in issuing to them provisions and ammunition. The delay at the river was greater than I wished, yet, I trust, justifiable, as it was, in part, occasioned by the request of General St. Clair, which you will find by referring to the extract of his letter, contained in No. 1. ...

On the morning of the 1st instant, as the army entered an extensive prairie, I perceived an Indian on horse-back, a few miles to the right; I immediately made a detachment to intercept him, but he escaped; finding myself discovered, I determined to advance with all the rapidity my circumstances would permit, rather with the hope than the expectation of reaching the object sought that day: for my guides were strangers to the country which I occupied. At one o'clock, having marched, by computation, one hundred and fifty-five miles to the Ohio, as I penetrated a grove which bordered on an extensive prairie, I discovered two small villages to my left, at two and four miles distance. ...

The enemy still kept possession of the Kickapoo town; I determined to dislodge them, and for that purpose ordered Captain King's and Logsdon's companies to march down the river below the town, and cross, under the conduct of Major Barbee...I immediately detached Captain Brown, with his company, to support the Colonel; but the distance being six miles, before the Captain arrived, the business was done, and Colonel Hardin joined me a little before sunset, having killed six warriors, and taken fifty-two prisoners...

On the 4th, I determined to discharge sixteen of the weakest and most infirm of my prisoners, with a talk to the Wabash tribes, a copy of which you will find enclosed in No. 4. ...

[132] On the same day, after having burned the towns and adjacent villages, and destroyed the growing corn and pulse, I began my march for the rapids of Ohio, where I arrived the 14th inst. without the loss of a single man by the enemy, and five only wounded, having killed thirty-two, chiefly warriors of size and figure, and taken fifty eight prisoners.

It is with much pride and pleasure I mention, that no act of inhumanity has marked the conduct of the volunteers of Kentucky on this occasion; even the inveterate habit of scalping the dead, ceased to influence.

I have delivered forty-one prisoners to Captain Asheton, of the 1st United States' regiment, at Fort Steuben, for which I have his receipt, as per the enclosed copy in No. 5. ...

CHARLES SCOTT, B. G.

To the Honorable Councill now sitting in Boston

The petition of William Waldron

Humbly showeth unto yr Honr that whereas yor Petitioner is committed to prison by your order of the Honr Councell as by ye attest of Mr Edward Rwnson Secret for Seizing and not Long since conveighing away a Sagamore Indian and other Indians to ye Eastward to Fyall or other Islands beyond Sea, yor petitioner is able to produce Sufficient Testimony to prove yt he was not further to the eastward then Menhegnme, and Damaras-Cove, which is not so farre Eastward by a hundred and fifty Leagues, as ye place is where ye Indians was taken from, as the Report Goes, and yt he was Ignorant yt any was taken away, brother did he define or wish or order any pson or psons whatsoever to molest or take away any Indian from any part to the eastward except Indian Enemies according to the Tenr of his Commission neither Could he order any such thing if he would. And if it be so yt any Indians is taken away by any person or persons whatsoever unlegally its fitt yt they should Suffer and not [illegible], yt neither wished it nor desired it nor Could order it, but am wholly Ignorant of the Same and also why I Should be Retained and and kept in prison form my buisness which is so great a prejudice to me yt I cannot express it, and withall no Benefitt to the Country, Wherefore the Request of yor Humble Petitioner is yt he may forthwith be Called to a tryall or that Baile may be taken for his appearance at the next County Court, or when yor Honr Shall be pleased to Call him to Answer to his Tryall, which if yor Honble health and prosperity ever pray etc

24 August 1676

The Council Court Grant [illegible] report

E. R. S

Will Waldron

This indenture witnesseth that John Pagatoon, Indian man, and Sarah, Indian woman, by and with the consent of their master Thomas Reeves of Southold on Long Island have put and bound themselves servants to Joseph Bigelow of Hartford in the Colony of Connecticut after the manner of servants faithfully to serve him for and during the full term of five years to begin at the date hereof during all which time the said servants shall faithfully serve their said master his heirs or assigns his lawful commands obey. They shall do no damage to their said master nor see it done by others without giving notice thereof to said master. They shall not absent themselves by night or day from their said master’s service without his consent (which if they do they shall serve him threble the time of their so absenting themselves and also pay threble damages), but in all things shall behave themselves as good and faithful servants ought to do during said term.

Furthermore, the said John Pagatoon and Sarah, his wife, parents to Sampson, Indian boy, by and with the consent and advice of their said master Thomas Reeves do bind their said son, Sampson, a servant to said Joseph Bigelow for and during the full term nineteen years and an half or until he shall be of the age of twenty and one years. During all which term or time the Sampson shall faithfully serve the said Joseph Bigelow, his master, his lawful commands obey he shall do no damage to his said master nor see it done without giving notice thereof to his said master. He shall not absent himself from his master’s service by day or night without his leave or consent, but in all things behave himself as a good and faithful servant ought to do during the said term. And the said Joseph Bigelow shall procure and provide for his said servants sufficient meat and drink, apparel and lodging suitable for his servants and on the account of said John Pagatoon and Sarah shall pay and satisfy to the said Thomas Reave fifty pounds money, a debt due from said John and Sarah to said Reaves and shall give and deliver to the said Sampson at the expiration of his term of service a horse that shall be then valued at five pounds money. And for the fine performance of every of the covenant and agreements therein contained every of the parties bind themselves each to the other firmly by these presents; in witness whereof they and each of them have hereunto set their hands and seals this twelfth day of July, Anno Domini 1723 Annoq RR Georgii Novo

Sign, sealed and delivered in presence of us.

record_transcription:
Fifty Dollars Reward.

RUNAWAY from the Subscriber, on Saturday night the 2d instant, one Negro Man named Sam, and one Negro Woman named Kate. Sam is of a yellow complexion, about 5 feet 8 inches high, slender built, about 28 years old, has two of his fore teeth a little defected, and has a bushy head, a little inclined to Indian. He carried away with him sundry home cloaths, some striped and some mixed, also one striped Swansdown waistcoat, made a few days before he started. Kate is of a dark complexion, about 30 or 35 years of age, of a common size. She has several of her fore teeth out. She carried away with her sundry cloathing, mostly homespun and that striped.

I have some expectation they will try to get to Norfolk or Baltimore, in one of which towns Kate was raised. Sam has no connection, but at my house, having partly raised him myself, and at this time own his father and mother. Kate I purchased of Mr. Thos.[Thomas] Hancock, of Smithfield in Virginia, about two years ago. Any person who will deliver the said Negroes to me, or to John Stephens, jun, of Smithfield, N C shall receive 25 dollars, and all reasonable expences paid, if taken within the State ; and it taken without the State, 50 dollars. Or any person who will apprehend and lodge them in any Jail, so that I get them again, shall be well rewarded for their trouble.

Any information given to me, or to Mr. John Stevens, jun. in Smithfield, of the route they have taken, will be thankfully recieved. All masters of vessels, and others, are cautioned against harbouring, employing, or carrying them away, at their peril.

BARNABY BULLS.

Johnston County, N.C. 10 miles below Smithfield, March 4

[14] Saturday the 6th Day of June 1724

The House mett according to Adjournment ———

Mr Secretary Hart brought from his Exe’cy the Governr.. the following Message———

...

[15] The way of getting Men for the Garrisons I take to be not onely inconvenient but verry unsafe therefore the sooner these things are Consider’d the better and I shall assist the Committee therein and now that the honble Collo.. Chicken is Commissionr.. of the Indian affaires and Supervisr.. of the—Garrisons that all Letters and Pson’s concern’d be Sent to him for by their soe doing these affaires will the sooner be dispatchd’ & with less trouble as for the three Indians they brought down to me I propose to keep two of them to Send as presents to their Royal highness’s the Prince and Princess of Whales and have enquird of those concernd’ in Indian Trade who say they may sell for abt fifty pounds a peice wherefore to Ease the Country the Charge of the Indians I Shall give them One hundred pounds & I propose That the other Indian may be Sold toward defraying the charge & as for the Skin’s a present to me I would have them sold to the best advantage toward defraying the Charge of the Indians

honrble Gentlm..

[225-227] Upon the Petition of Jonathan Hall Junr. Elam Cook and Abigail his Wife Samuel Talmadge and Phebe his Wife all of Cheshire and David Hall of Essex in the State of Vermont Children and Heirs to Joseph Hall late of said Cheshire Deceasd said Elam and Samuel in Right of their said Wives Shewing to this Assembly, That on the 6th Day of April 1751, said Joseph then being in full Life purchased of Stephen Judd late of said Waterbury Deceased then in full Life an Indian Molletto Girl named Rhoda as and for a Slave for Life took her Home educated and brought her up and retained her in his Service for many Years during which Time she had a number of Children born in the House of said Joseph who was at great expence in taking Care of nursing and bringing them up during the Time they lived with him, that said Joseph afterwards sold said Rhoda together with Peter one of her Children to Joel Ives, who sold said Rhoda to David Hotchkiss, and said David, to Dick Bristol her husband with whom she now lives, and said Joel Ives sold said Peter to Samuel Clark, who sold him Samuel Bellamy who now holds him, said Joseph also sold Lilly another of the Children of said Rhoda to the Revd John Lewiss, who sold her to John Robbins Junr who now holds her, And said Joseph also sold George one of the other Children of said Rhoda to Daniel Plumb, who sold him to Richard Dowe late of Middletown Deceasd, in the distribution of whose Estate he was set to Samuel Wilcox who sold him to said John Robbins Junr who now holds him, And said Joseph at the Time of his Death left Hampton another of the Children of said Rhoda who came into the Hands of said Jonathan Hall Junr his Sons & Executor who sold him to Simeon Bristol Esqr. who sold him to Robert Martin late of said Cheshire Deceased, and upon his Decease came into the Hands of his Executors Samuel Clark & John Martin, that since the Decease of said Joseph said Hampton Claims to be free, and States that his Mother was born free and was the Daughter of a Spanish Squaw, And thereupon said Hampton brought forward a Suit at Law against said Jonathan for selling him as and for a Slave when he was Born, which Suit went through a Course of Law, and came to a final Tryal to the Jury before the Superior Court which terminated in favour of said Jonathan & against the Freedom of said Hampton, another Suit was afterwards brought by said Hampton for an Assault, against the Executors of said Robert Martin in which the same Question came up, and in a final Tryal to the Jury terminated in favour of the Freedom of Hampton, And the Question relative to the Freedom of said Negroes has had various and contradictory determinations in the Courts of Law, There is also a Suit in Law now pending between said Bristol and said Jonathan relative to the same Question, that it is evident from the aforesaid Statement of Facts, that if all the various Claims of these Negroes and the several Purchasers and sundry other Persons, And the uncertainty which attends the Proof relative to the true Origin of Descent of said Rhoda, as there is no Person to be found who can from their own knoledge inform who was the Mother of said Rhoda, it is altogether probably there will be contradictory Judgments in the Courts of Law Praying this Assembly by themselves or a wise and Judicious Committee to examine into the Facts stated in said Petition and if said Rhoda shall be found to have been Free born that she and her Children should be Liberated and set free, and to adjust and settle all the Claims which the several Purchasers have in Justice & equity upon each other and to decree Payment; but if said Rhoda shall be found not to have been free born to Quiet the several Purchasers as per Petition on file &c

Resolved by this Assembly That the Honble Stephen Mix Mitchell Esqr, Jonathan Ingersol and Asher Miller Esquires be and they are hereby appointed a Committee with full Power and Authority, after giveing due and reasonable Notice to all Parties and Persons any way interested concerned or affected thereby to appear if they see Cause, to hear inquire and examine into the Facts Stated in said Petition, and make Report thereof with their Opinion what ought in Equity and Justice to be done thereon to make a final end of all said Controversies, and to quiet all Parties concerned therein, to the General Assembly to be holden at Hartford in May next, or to the General Assembly to be holden at New Haven in October next.

The humble petition of George Speere to the honored council humbly showeth

That your petitioner had bought an Indian boy of Capt. Hull, who by the honorable council was empowered to make sale of the Indian at that time: also bestowed two yeares care & education of him to prepare him for my service wch tooke good efort he being be brought to be very teachable and hopeful to be serviceable after all: wch care & charge it pleased: your honor by a warrant to ye constable of Braintree to take ye boy from me and deliver him to an Indian wch was soe against the boys will who tried & strove to his utmost against it & I believed had rather have lost his life than to have gone from me with them: I had so gained on his affections wch indeed makes my loss the greater for I esteemed him better than ye best black that I could have bought wch would have cost neere 30 beside my great disappointment in the want of his service having the improvement of a considerable farme under my hand. My humble request to your honor is that you would be pleased to consider my case & acordinge to your hon gracious promise in the warrant sent for the boy that upon my application to your honor you will order me satisfaction wch in this my application I humbly plead: beseechinge that what you please to graunt me may be money I having paid money for the boy if I had enjoyed would have been better to me than money: not doubting of your clemency to heare and also to relieve in so just a case by your favorable answer to my request for wch I humbly waite & subscribe my selfe

your Hon most humble suppliant & servant

George Speere

Fifty Dollars Reward.

RANAWAY from the Subscriber, in the month of January last, a negro man named JACK, and his Wife named ESTHER. The former is a Carpenter, about 40 years old, six feet high, black, speaks quick; the woman is about 30 years old, low, and of an Indian complection, said to have Indian blood. I bought them from Col. Joyner, of Sampson, a short time before they ranaway. Jack was originally purchased from Mr. Edwards, of Greene County, to which neighborhood they may have returned, but it is more likely that they have gone to Florida, near Quincey. The above reward will be paid for their apprehension and confinement in any Jail, so that I get them, or $20 for any information that may lead to their recovery.

HEROLD BLACKMORE.

Duplin County, Sept. 10, 1835.

She was brought up by own Greene at Narraganset, and is called Hannah Greene, but 'tis probable she will change her Name: She had on and carried with her, a dark striped flannel Gown, and a striped linnen Ditto, two Quilts, and sundry other Cloathing; 'tis probable she may have gone towards Albany & Crown Point, having as she says, been in a Campaign. Whoever will return said Servant, or give Information of her to her said Master, so that he may have her again, shall have necessary Charges paid them, if to the amount of TEN POUNDS lawful Money, besides a handsome Reward; in proportion to their Trouble, paid by ALEXANDER McNEILL, New London, Jan. 23d, 1766.

[5] INDENTURING INDIANS - A NICE SYSTEM OF SLAVERY.

RED BLUFF, January 30, 1861.

EDITORS UNION: As the meaning and intent, as well as the consitutionality of the Act passed last Winter in regard to indenturing Indians without their consent, or even apprising them of the fact, but by simply calling on the County or District Judge, with a list, and having him sign it officially-has been doubted by many, I send you a copy of an indenture, now on file in the Clerk's office in Tehama county. The Indians named therein are not prisoners of war, or vagrant Indians, but belong to the Nome Lackee tribe, that have been taught to work, at a cost to Government of about three hundred thousand dollars. And the persons to whom they are indentured have been receiving as salaries from Government, four hundred and seventy-five dollars per month, for nearly four years past.

It may be true that they were in their possesion at that date, as they claimed to be in possession of the Reserve. They were most of them on the Reservation, and not ten per cent. of them have ever seen their humane (?) guardian that "at the instance and request" of Titus and Geiger, made them slaves, without the semblance of a bond to clothe, feed and protect them.

I hope our representatives from this country will attend to this law, and have it either explained or repealed.

record_transcription: [322] Being shown to a well-furnished room, we changed our travel-soiled clothing for a more civilized costume, by which time breakfast was announced, and we were ushered into a large dining-hall. In the centre stood a table, upon which was spread a substantial breakfast of stewed and fried beef, fried onions, and potatoes, bread, butter, and coffee. Our appetites were very sharp, and we did full justice to the merits of the fare before us. The servants waiting upon the table were an Indian muchachito and muchachita, about ten or twelve years of age. They had not been long from their wild rancherias, and knew but little of civilized life. Our host, however, who speaks, I believe, nearly every living language, whether Christian, barbarian, or savage nations, seemed determined to impress upon their dull intellects the forms and customs of civilization.

[456-458] JOHN WINTHROP TO WILLIAM BRADFORD

WORTHY SIR, I receiued your louing letter, and am much prouocked to express my affections towards you, but straitnes of time forbids me, for my desire is to acquainte you, with the lords greate mercies towards vs, in our preuailing against his, and our enimies; that you may rejoyce, and praise his name with vs. About 80 of our men haueing costed along towards the dutch plantation, (some times by water, but most by land) mett hear, and ther, with some pequents, whom they slew or tooke prisoners. 2 sachems they tooke, and beheaded And not hearing of Sassacous (the cheefe sachem) they gaue a prisoner his life, to goe and find him out. He wente and brought them word wher he was, but Sassacouse suspecting him to be a spie, after he was gone fled away, with some 20 more, to the Mohawkes; so our men missed of him. yet deviding them seules, and ranging vp and downe, as the providence of God guided them (for the Indeans were all gone, saue 3 or 4 And they knew not whither to guid them, or els would not) vpon the 13 of this month, they light vpon a great company of them viz. 80 strong men, and 200 women, and children in a small Indean towne, fast by a hideous swamp, which they all slipped Into before our men could gett to them. Our captains were not then come together, but ther was mr. Ludlow, and Captaine Masson, with some 10 of their men, and Captaine Patrick with some 20 or more of his; who shooting at the Indeans, Captaine Trask with 50 more came soone in at the noyse; then they gaue order to surround the swampe, it being aboute a mile aboute; but Leutenante Dauenporte, and some 12 more, not hearing that cammand, fell into the swampe among the Indeans. the swampe was so thicke with shrub woode, and so boggie with all, that some of them stuck fast, and receiued many shott. Leutenant Dauenport was dangerously wounded about his armehole and another shott in the head, so as fainting, they were in great danger to haue been taken by the Indeans; but Sargante Rigges, and Jeffery and 2 or 3 more rescued them, and slew diuerse of the Indeans, with their swords. After they were drawne out, the Indeans desired parley; and were offered (by Thomas Stanton, our Interpretour) that if they would come out, and yeeld them selues, they should haue their liues all that had not their hands in the English blood; whervpon the sachem of the place came forth, and an old man or 2 and theri wiues and chilldren; and after that some other women and children, and so they spake 2 howers, till it was night. then Thomas Stanton was sente into them againe, to call them forth; but they said, they would selle theri liues their, and so shott at him so thicke, as If he had not cried out, and been presently rescued, they had slaine him. Then our men cutt of a place of the swampe with their swords, and cooped the Indeans into so narrow a compass, as they could easier kill them throw the thikets; so they continued all the night, standing aboute 12 foote from an other, and the Indeans coming close vp to our men, shot their arrows so thicke, as they peirced their hatte brimes, and their sleeues and stockins, and other parts of their cloaths, yet so miraculously did the lord preserue them, as not one of them was wounded, saue those 3 who rashly went into the swampe. When it was nere day, it grue very darke, so as those of whem which were left, dropt away betweene our men, though they stood but 12 or 14 foote assunder; but were presenly discouered, and some killed in the pursute. Vpon searching of the swampe the next morning, they found 9 slaine, and some they pulled vp, whome the Indeans had buried in the mire; so as they doe thinke that, of all this company, not 20 did escape, for after they found some, who dyed in their flight, of their wounds receiued. The prisoners were devided, some to those of the riuer, and the rest to vs; of these we send the male children to Bermuda, by mr. William Peirce, and the women and maid children are disposed aboute in the townes. Ther haue been now slaine and taken in all aboute 700. The rest are dispersed, and the Indeans in all quarters so terrified, as all their freinds are affraid to receiue them. 2 of the Sachems of long Iland came to mr. Stoughton and tendered them selues to be tributaries, vnder our protection. And 2 of the Neepnett Sachems haue been with me to seeke our friendship. Amonge the prisoners we haue the wife and children of Mononotto, a womon of a very modest countenance and behaviour. It was by her mediation they they 2 English maids were spared from death, and were kindly vsed by her; so that I haue taken charge of her. One of her first requests was that the English would not abuse her body and that her children might not be taken from her. Those which were wounded were fetched of soone by John Galopp who came with his shalop in a hippie houre, to bring them victuals, and to carrie their wounded men to the pinnass, wher our cheefe surgeon was, mr. Willson, being aboute 8 leagues of. Our people are all in health (the lord be praised) and allthough they had marched in their armes all the day, and had been in fight all the night, yet they professed they found them selues so fresh as they could willingly haue gone to such another bussines.

This is the substance of that which I receiued, though I am forced to omite many considerable circomstances. So being in much straitnes of time (the ship being to departe within this 4 days, and in them the Lord Lee and mr. Vane) I hear breake of, and with harty saluts to, etc. I rest Yours assured

JO: WINTHROP

the 28 of the 5 month 1637

The captains reporte, we haue slaine 13 sachems; but Sassacouse and Monotto are yet liuing.

record_transcription: October 26. An Indian or Mustee fellow, about 36 years of age, named SIMON FLOWERS, has a small beard, and born at Santee, says he is free, (but has nothing to prove it) that his father and mother were Indians, named Tom and Betty Flowers, his father dead, but his mother alive, has two brothers named Ben and Will, they all live on Santee. He says when he was little his father bound him to one John Thomas, who lives six miles over Santee river (near John Morrice and Stephen Willes, planters) and that all his relations live close by; he says his master has used him very ill, and would not let him go when his time was out, but intended to keep him as a slave.—He is marked on the right cheek W, on his left with a single stroke thus 1, which he says his father did to all his children when they were small, with a needle and gunpowder: He has on an old negro cloth jacket, dyed yellow, blue breeches, osnaburgh shirt, and has been whipped very much about his back. Taken up at Mr George Marshall's up the path.

The petition of Jonathan Fairebankes

record_transcription:
[115] MARY GRAYSON

Age 83 yrs.

Tulsa, Oklahoma

I am what we colored people call a "native.” That means that I didn't come into the Indian country from somewhere in the Old South, after the War, like so many negroes did, but I was born here in the old Creek Nation, and my master was a Creek Indian. That was eighty three years ago, so I am told.

My mammy belonged to white people back in Alabama when she was born — down in the southern part I think, for she told me that after she was a sizeable girl her white people moved into the eastern part of Alabama where there was a lot of Creeks. ...

A Creek come to my mammy's master and bought her to bring out here, but she heard she was being sold and run off into the woods. There was an old clay pit, dug way back into a high bank, where the slaves had been getting clay to mix with hog hair scrapings to make chinking for the big log houses that they built for the master and the cabins they made for themselves. Well, my mammy run and hid way back in that old clay pit, and it was way after dark before the master and the other man found her. ... He took her away and was kind to her, but he decided she was too young to breed and he sold her to another Creek...

[116] One of the bunch, named Jim Perryman, bought my mammy and married her to one of his "boys", but after he waited a while and she didn't have a baby he decided she was no good breeder and he sold her to Mose Perryman.

Mose Perryman was my master, and he was a cousin to Legus Perryman, who was a big man in the tribe. He was a lot younger than Mose, and laughed at Mose for buying my mammy, but he got fooled, because my mammy got married to Mose's slave boy Jacob, the way the slaves was married them days, and went ahead and had ten children for Mr. Mose. ...

When I was born we lived in the Choska bottoms...

[119] "Your pappy and your Uncle Hector and your Uncle William and a lot of other menfolks won't be here any more. They went away." ...

[121] Then one day Mr. Mose came and told us that the War was over and that we would have to root for ourselves after that. But he just rode away and I never saw him after that until after we had got back into the Choska country. ...

[122] When we got to the Agency mammy met a Negro who had seen pappy and knew where he was, so we sent word to him and he came and found us. He had been through most of the War in the Union army.

[123] When I got to be a young woman I went to Okmulgee and worked for some people near there for several years, then I married Tate Grayson. We got our freedmen's allotments on Mingo Creek, east of Tulsa, and lived there until our children were grown and Tate died, then I came to live with my daughter in Tulsa.

On the 29th of November, 1690, a truce or treaty of peace was made by the government of Massachusetts "with the eastern Indian enemy, sagamores," among whom was John Hawkins. The sagamores, six in number, "covenant, promise and agree for themselves, and all the eastward Indians now in open hostility with the English--from the Pennecook, Winnepesseockeege, Ossipe, Pigwocket, Amoscongin, Pechepscut, Kennebeck river"--to keep the peace, &c. GENERAL NEWS.

FROM KANSAS.

A CREEK INDIAN KIDNAPPED AND ENSLAVED.

Correspondence of the Cincinnati Gazette.

QUINDARO, Kansas, Sept. 1.

Ox yokes are manufactured in Kansas almost by the cord for the Government trains to Utah. A Creek Indian, whose father was a mulatto, has been manufacturing them extensively at Quindaro, having a number of men at work for him. A week ago yesterday, he went down with his team to move a family from Johnson county, Kansas and when about ten miles below this place, the wagon was suddenly surrounded by a body of armed men from Missouri, who claimed our Creek Indian as a fugitive slave from that state. Great excitement was created at Quindaro by the news of this kidnapping, but nothing could be learned of the Creek until yesterday, when it was ascertained that he was in jail at Independence Mo. on the affidavit of a wealthy citizen of that State, that he had been found running at large in the State of Missouri, with out an owner. The truth was, he had not been within ten miles of the Missouri line, and was arrested at least a dozen miles from the border.

The man has free papers from the Indian Agent. His mother was an Indian woman and there is no pretext for claiming him as a slave. John W Wright, attorney at law at Quindaro, went down yesterday to get a writ of habeas corpus. Whether the Missourians wil be able to scare him out, you can judge. You know him better than I do. He came here from Logansport, Ind. and is the man that whipped Vallette in Cincinnati.

If Indian and free negroes are to be kidnapped in this way on the free soil of Kansas, you need not wonder if our citizens retaliate by putting the underground in operation, and running it clear into Missouri. KANSAS.

All persons, (and every person) are hereby notified, that on Sunday before Easter the subscriber was in possession, by virtue of a purchase from the real Administrator of William M'Cullough, deceased, a certain Negro called Arnold, aged about 20 years-- which said Negro missing, and has been ever since. Said Negro is about 5 feet 5 nches high of a copper colour, supposed of Indian extraction, round face, low forehead, small black eyes, pretty well set and talkative. Had on when he went away a pair of thickset breeches, much worn and pieced on the seat with grey cloth, a new brown cloth outside jacket, and supposed to be carried off secretly for sale by on John Merchant, a stout portly man, with a large mark on one side of his face and cheek. From some previous expressions of said Merchant of such intent, and both being missing, any person who will secure in any jail the said Negro Arnold or bring him to the subscriber at Oyster-Shell Town, Maryland, shall be handsomely rewarded for the same --- All persons are hereby forbid buying the above Negro from said Merchant, or any other than the subscriber.

ESME MERILL. Somerset County, Maryland. Feb. 18, 1798.

To John Richards Esqrone of His Majesty's Justices of the peace for the County of New London

Stephen Gardner of Norwich in Sd. County here by Informes & Complains That Cesar a Molatto Man Servant And Ann a Spanish Indian Squaw And Ann an Indian Girl and Phillis an Indian Girl att which are Servants and Slaves To the Complainant, in the Night Next after the 3d. Instant Contrary To them Retainer Deserted their Sd. Masters Service in Norwich aforsd. the Complainant therefore prayes process against the Said fugative Servants and that they may be Arrested and brought before Your worship and further dealt with According To Law

Norwich, October the 4th 1743 Stephen Gardiner

To the Sheriff of New London County his Deputy or Either of the Constables of the Towns of New London or Norwich within Said County Greeting Stephen Gardiner of Sd. Norwich, came before me the Subscribers one of his Majesty's Justices of the peace for the County of New London & Complaines that Cesar, Ann, and Ann, and Philiss his Indian & Molatto Servants and Slaves on the Night Next after the sd. Instant in Norwich, aforsd. Deserted there Masters Service contrary To them Retainer and hath pray'd process against the Said fugative Servants and Slaves that they may be Arrested and dealt with According To Law as pr. Complaint on file, Dated Octor. 4th 1743

These are Therefore In his Majesty's Name To command You or Either of Your or [?]erts. thereof the Body's of the Sd. Cesar, & Ann, & Ann and Philiss, To Arrest and them forth with bring before me the Subscribers at the Dwelling house of the Said Stephen Gardiner in Norwich aforsd. To be Examined upon the premises and further dealt with as the Law Directs fail not and Lawfull Return Make of this writt with your Doings thereon Dated at New London October the 6th Day Anno.

Dom: 1743 John Gardiner Just. Pecs.

The foregoing and True Coppys as on file

Examined pr. John Richards Just. Pecs.

Novembr Term [Second?] 1743 and Now the Defendts Comes into Court and Defends and Says that they Are not Guilty in manner and forme and thereof that them selves upon the Country Backus Lee for me Defents

and the plantif in Like maner [illegible] for plantif

At a Court held in Norwich in the County of New London before John Richards one of his Majesty's Justices of the peace forsd. County October the 6th Day of A.D. 1743

Cesar A Molatto man, And Ann an Indian Spanish Squaw & Ann An Indian Girl and Philis An Indian Girl all Servants and Slaves unto Stephen Gardiner of Said Norwich being arrested and brought before this Court to Answer the Complaint of the Said Stephen Gardiner, who Complaines that all the Sd. Servants And Slaves contrary To their Retainer on the Night, Next following the 3d. Day of October Instant deserted his Service, &c as pr. [?]eutt and Complaint on file, Dated October 6th. 1743

And the Said Ann the Eldest, and Ann and Philiss and Cesar Came into This Court and pleaded as follows that the Said Ann the Eldest was a Mohawk Squaw and born free, and that the Said Cesar and Ann the Younger and Philliss were born of her the Said Ann the Eldest, and therefore ought not to be holden in Service, &c and they were heard in their pleas and the Case being above the province of this Court to determine, it is Considered by this Court that the Said Cesar Ann and Ann and Philiss hath become bound with Sufficient Surety in the penall Sum of Two Hundred and Fifty pounds Lawfull Money of this Colony of Connecticut to the Treasr. of the County of New London by way of Recognizance that the Said Cesar Ann, & Ann, & Phillis and Each of them the sd. Servants & Slaves Shall Answer at the County Court to be holden at Norwich, within [?] for the County of New London on the fourth Tuesday of November Next, and Answer the sd. Elizabeth Rogers ^of Lawfull age the wife of Jonathan Rogers Son of Samuel Rogers Decd Testifieth that about four years ago, a young Indian Woman Servt to Stephen Gardiner of Norwich was at our house in order to be Cured of a Sore She had & Stayed about three Weeks, in which time a She told me She was a Servt to the Sd Gardiner and that her mother was a Slave and was a Spanish Indian or what I understood to be a Spanish Indian & that She was of the Same Country with Indian John who was a Servt to mr. Livingstone Late of New London Decd. and in a few months after that an Indian Woman came to our house and told me that her name was Ann & that She was a Servt to Stephn Gardiner of Norwich and that She was the mother of that Ann that had been Lately at our house to be Cared and that She was a Spanish Indian of the Same Country with Indian John who was Mr. Livingstones Servant

NewLondon So November the 28th . 1743 the above named Elizabeth Rogers (not being able to attend the Court by Reason of Bodyly Infirmity.) made oath to the above written evidence, (the adverse party being notified but not present before me J: Hempsted Justice of the Peace

New London In Norwich[?] at a County Court Novr [?] 1743: this Evidence was[?] into Court and was opend in Court pr Isaac Huntington Just of ye [illegible]

Abigail Powers aged upwards of Sixty years Testifieth that about 28 or 29 years ago I Lived at the ferry at Boston neck in the Naharagansit Country, and then and there I most well aquainted Ann an Indian woman, Now Suing for her freedom from Stephn Gardiner of Norwich, I Saw her & Spoke with her when She was ^at the house of Justice Richards in New London this fall I Supose in September Last. when I first Saw her it was at Brother William Gardiners at Sd Boston Neck he had newly bought her at Newport and Divers others were brought over from Newport for Several other persons at the Same time and they were all Called Spanish Indians & So Esteemed & understood by us & the neighbors, this Same Ann I was Invited by Brother ^William Gardiner to buy her but She was not in good health & I Refused, and afterward in a few Days Stephen Gardiner abovesd bought her of his Brother William & She hath Lived with Brother Stephen Gardiner Ever Since till this fally & hath had Several Children Two Sons one named Cesar & one abraham, that I was aquainted with & the other Children I was not acquainted with. I very well Remember that the Sd. Ann had a Strake on one of her Leggs down her Shin in her gartering place flowered after the Indian fashion. I very well Remember her first Son was Born before the great Snow which was about 27 years ago

the abovenamed Abigail Powers made oath to the above written Evidence (She not being in health of Body to attend ye Court) the Adverse party being Notified but not present this 28th Day of November 1743

before me J: L: Hempsted Justice of Peace

The testimony of Martin Kellogg of Weathsfield aged fifty Seven years: testifies and Says that he has Lived Some years In Canada among the mohawks & french In Which time he got to Knowledg of a Considerable part of the mohawk Language Now having ^had opportunity to discourse With ann indi an Syman Said to be Claimed by Stephen Gardner as his slave: do finde that She talk Mohawk and according to the best of his understanding a hurone which nation is one of the five nations Caled: mohawk. and having asked her many Questions which She answered & ^in Mohawk without Shuting her Lips which is peculiar to the mohawk tribes Exampts of all other nations that Is Ever heard of the method he took Was to ask her many questions over night all Which he Writ down with Every ans wer therto & Called ye aforesd, ann the next morn ing askt her ye Same questions over again to which She made ye Same answer/ In mohawk

martin Kellogg

The testimony of Rebecca Kellogg aged forty Seven years testifies and Says that She lived twenty four years among the mohawk In Cannada In which - time She Learnt the mohawk tongue and now having had opportunity to discourse with ann indian Squaw Said to be Claimed by Stephen Gardner of norridg as his Slave: do finde that She talks mohawk and according to the best of her Judgement She is one of the Hurone which nation is one of the five nations Caled mohawk & Says She askt ye sd ann indian Squaw many questions In mohawk Which Sd ann answered in mohawk Without Shutting her Lips Which She thinks is peculiar to the Mohawk tribe Exempt of all other tribes She Know's Her

Rebecca Kellogg

[5] INDENTURING INDIANS - A NICE SYSTEM OF SLAVERY.

RED BLUFF, January 30, 1861.

EDITORS UNION: As the meaning and intent, as well as the consitutionality of the Act passed last Winter in regard to indenturing Indians without their consent, or even apprising them of the fact, but by simply calling on the County or District Judge, with a list, and having him sign it officially-has been doubted by many, I send you a copy of an indenture, now on file in the Clerk's office in Tehama county. The Indians named therein are not prisoners of war, or vagrant Indians, but belong to the Nome Lackee tribe, that have been taught to work, at a cost to Government of about three hundred thousand dollars. And the persons to whom they are indentured have been receiving as salaries from Government, four hundred and seventy-five dollars per month, for nearly four years past.

It may be true that they were in their possesion at that date, as they claimed to be in possession of the Reserve. They were most of them on the Reservation, and not ten per cent. of them have ever seen their humane (?) guardian that "at the instance and request" of Titus and Geiger, made them slaves, without the semblance of a bond to clothe, feed and protect them.

I hope our representatives from this country will attend to this law, and have it either explained or repealed.

(264) Ammerman dropped the petition when Jack filed an indenture for another Apache minor, Guillermo (Gavilan) Swilling, a boy he favored enough to pass onto him his surname. In filing this legal claim to Guillermo's services, Jack effectively barred other neighbors and "friends" from interfering with his Native wards during the aftermath of the Camp Grant Massacre, during which American, Mexican, and O'odham men killed more than 140 Apaches camped along Aravaipa Creek. [...] Swilling's indenture of Gavilan may have been a protective gesture meant to shield his indigenous children from the anti-Apache sentiment growing among his neighbors.

That Justice Swilling favored Guillermo was made most evident in a studio photograph taken of the boy and his patron around 1875.

(265) [...] Biographer Al Bates claims that Trinidad explained the photo as a family joke, meant to poke fun by overplaying Jack's desperado image and posing Guillermo as his fierce Indian bodyguard. Regardless of the justice's intent, the image clearly depicts the slippage between bonds of indenture and bonds of affection that the Howell Code aimed to discourage. [...]

(267) [...] In their biographies, Bates and Wilson recognize Guillermo's presence in Swilling's household, though neither acknowledges Bonifacio and Guadalupa Woolsey or Mariana, the three other Indian children who appeared in Swilling's census records. Bates claims that the Confederate indentured Guillermo because adoption was not allowed under the legal code until 1873, supporting the notion that Jack used indenture as a protective and paternalist measure.

[...]

(272) [...] Gavilan Pollero, minor child of a "hostile Indian tribe," became Guillermo Swilling [...]

He shall not waste his s'd master or mistresses goods nor Lend them unlawfully to any: he shall not commit fornication nor contract matrimony within s'd term: No Cards Dice or any other unlawful Game He shall not play whereby his s'd master or mistress may have Damage with his own goods or y' goods of others He shall not absent himself by day or by Night from his s'd master or mistresses service without their Leave no haunt ale houses taverns or play houses; but in all things behave himself as a faithfull Apprentice ought to do towards his s'd master or mistress & all theirs During y' s'd term, And the s'd Giddeon Gifford & Elizabeth Gifford his wife for them selves & their heirs Doth here by Covenant & promise to teach & instruct or Cause y' s'd apprentice to be taught & Instructed in y' art trade or calling of a house carpenter by the best ways or means he or they can within y' s'd term finding unto ye s'd apprentice good & sufficient meat drink apperel washing & lodging suitable for for such an apprintice both in sickness & in helth During s'd term & also to Teach or Cause y' s'd apprintice to be taught to Read & Wright English with In the s'd term And at y' Expiration to give unto y' s'd apprintice one good New suite of apperel for all parts of his body besides his Daily wareing cloths And as many carpenters tools of such sorts as he shall Chose as shall be worth three pounds old tenner &c. In the presence of Job Gifford, Gideon Gifford, Jabez Gibbs, Elizabeth Gifford

Indictment of Indian Dick, a servant of Peleg Smith, Esq. for having made an assault on John Davis of Newport, baker, 25 December 1724 in the house of one Mary Silverwood in Newport and wounded him in the left hand with a sharp knife so that he was greatly disabled, &c; Daniel Updike, attorney. John Davis stated that he was passing by the house of Mary Silverwood, and "was desired to go up into her Chamber and suppress anoyes and Disturbance there ... [when he] came up there was Dick an Indian belonging unto Peleg Smith Esq. and Boston an Indian belonging to Mr. Peter Treby and Worwick an Indian belonging to Edward Thurston, Esq. ... wass some Squas in the Chamber which I did not know ... Dick struck att me with a knife and cutt me acrose the hand and rist of ye aposite hand." Dick, in his statement, said that he was quarrelling with Tom, a Negro belonging to Major Brown about a squaw and mistook Davis for Tom. Tom stated that the "week before last I sea Mary Silverwood by the Watch house and she asked me to come to her house on Cristmas Day night." Boston under examination said that they "had ale and punch at Silverwoods and [he] spent 3s ... took a knife away from Dick ... did not known Mr. Davis was cutt until this morning...there was Alce Frye and Judey tht lives with James Brown Jnr." Toney, a Negro belonging to Mr. Daniel White, was questioned and said that he was at Mary Silverwoods last Friday night and Tom and Dick quarrelled about squaws... "Mrs. Silverwood desired James Cadman a free negro to walk up in the chamber and prevent there quarriling...sd James belongs to Mr. Rodman. We Disired them to walk Down but they would not and Mr. Rodmans Negro tuke of Dicks hatt and Run down Stayors and the Indian follow...Dick said he would not go Down so James Cadman went to Putt him Down Stayors...James was Cutt...Mr. John Davis came up and the Candell I think was out when Mr. Davis was Cutt...I went away presently after to John Butmans a negro...."

[430] The Attestation of Capt. Edward STANYAN taken 10 Aug 1658 under his own hand as follows:

I, Edward STANYAN, being in my bed at eleven o’clock at night (by judgement) heard Goodman LINDITHE’s boy tell my wife that Paul TRIMINGHAM desired me to make haste to recover my boat for she was taken away. And all Mrs. TRIMINGHAM’s Indians were fled, and he would go ahead to Spanish Point to procure a boat to waylay them if possible. In the mean time, Lt. fforster came into my house with an iron hook in his hand, and seemed much perplexed, and desired me to make haste and see if we could prevent them. So on our way we called in at Mr. ELWICKE’s and got some powder for my pistol, and after at Henery JONES for lead to make shot. And Lt. ffORSTER, Matt NASH and I went out in Tho: MORRIS’ boat with six hands more, and lay off Ireland [Island] point until day, and seeing no boat at sea we returned home hopeless. And coming home, I was told that my boat was aground on the rocks and lay dangerously, and so I took posession of her [with the help of] the headburrow, and further saith not. Signed Edw. STANYAN 10 Aug 1658.

Twenty-five Dollars Reward.

RAN AWAY from the Subscriber, at his residence in Randolph county, N. C. on the 8th instant, Two young Negro Men, viz. JESSE and ELIJAH. Jesse is about twenty-two years old, weighs about 140 pounds, of low stature, but well made, is of dark mulatto color, and can read print tolerably well. Elijah is about eighteen years old, spare made, rather inclined to be slender built, and his lips project something beyond the proper length.--He had on when he left, a half-worn chip hat and thin homespun apparel. Both are intelligent, smart fellows, and will, no doubt, try to pass as free men, under the sir-name of Walden, Evans, or Chandler. They are partly Indian blood.

The above reward will be given for the apprehension and confinement of said Negroes in any Jail so that I get them again, or Twelve Dollars and Fifty Cents for either.

JNO. K. ARMISTEAD.

April 8, 1833.

This Indenture made the twenty Seventh day of the month Called Aprill in the year one Thousand Six hundred Seventy Eight Witneseth that William Cadman Samuell Wilbur and Robert Hodgson, all of the Town of Portsmouth in the Colony of Road Island and Providence plantations in New England, being by publick Authority appointed and Impowered to dispose of and place out Indians as apprentices in the Said Town of Portsmouth: have by these presents put, placed, and bound a certaine Indian girl now of the age of Six years or near Soe much who is Daughter of one meecquapew an Indian woman late of pocaset as an apprentice unto William Wodell of Portsmouth aforesaid and as an apprentice With the Said William Wodell his Executors, administrators and assigns to dwell for the full term and time of ffifteene years from the day of the date of these presents to bee Compleat and Ended by and dureing all which said time of fifteene years the Said Indian Girl whose name is Hannah Shall well and faithfully Serve her Said master William Wodell, his Executors, administrators, and assigns, in all Such lawfull busines as by him, them, or any of them Shee the Said Hannah Shall bee put to or Commanded to doe according to the best of her power Skill, and abillity and the Said William Wodell dureing all the Said terme Shall provide and allow, or cause to be provided and allowed unto his Said apprentice Sufficient food and Rayment and other nessessaries meet for Such an apprentice and at the End of the Said fifteene years Shall yield unto his said apprentice her freedome from this her Said Servitude

Witnes our hands and Seals

Wm Cadman Samuell Wilbur Robert Hodgson
